analysis.one_liner: Restores the right of U.S.-held detainees to challenge their detention in federal court.
analysis.headline: A bill restoring habeas corpus for detainees cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 26, 2007, but never received a Senate floor vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill repealed part of the Military Commissions Act of 2006, which had stripped federal courts of the power to hear habeas corpus challenges filed by non-citizens held by the United States as enemy combatants, including prisoners at Guantanamo Bay. Habeas corpus is the long-standing right to go before a judge and demand the government show a legal basis for holding you. The bill put that safeguard back in place for detained non-citizens and limited court review of military-commission trials to habeas cases and military law.
analysis.who_benefits: Foreign nationals detained by the United States as enemy combatants — including those held at Guantanamo Bay — would regain the right to go to federal court and make the government show a legal basis for their detention. Every person in U.S. custody also keeps the core safeguard against indefinite, unreviewable imprisonment.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provisions of the Military Commissions Act of 2006 that eliminated federal courts' jurisdiction over habeas corpus petitions from aliens detained as enemy combatants, restoring the habeas rights that existed before that law.
Lets courts consider legal challenges to military commissions only through military law or a habeas proceeding, preserving the prosecutions while re-opening the courts.
Applies to cases already pending, so detainees whose challenges were thrown out after the 2006 law could bring them back.

analysis.who_pays: The executive branch loses the power to hold non-citizens indefinitely without any court review, and the government bears the cost of litigating detention challenges in federal court.

drawbacks.text: The bill re-opens courtroom review of military detention decisions, meaning federal judges — not battlefield commanders — would second-guess who may be held as an enemy combatant, and litigation could burden the courts.
Because it applies to pending cases, detainees whose claims were already dismissed could restart litigation, prolonging legal fights over war-on-terror detentions.
Committee Republicans filed minority views alongside the favorable report, signaling organized opposition within the Judiciary Committee even before the bill reached the floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is restoring a constitutional safeguard — the right to have a court check the government before a person is held indefinitely — for a narrow group of detained non-citizens. The cost is real but ordinary: more litigation and judicial scrutiny of wartime detention decisions. This is the standard trade-off of habeas corpus, which has existed in Anglo-American law for centuries; the bill restores the pre-2006 status quo rather than creating a new entitlement.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill without amendment and placed it on the Senate calendar in June 2007, but it never came up for a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Arlen Specter (R-PA), the senior Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, with two dozen original cosponsors led by Democrats.
The Senate referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which held hearings on May 22, 2007.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably on June 7, 2007, and reported it without amendment on June 26, 2007, with written report No. 110-90 and additional and minority views filed.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 220 on June 26, 2007 — and no further action was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executive branch: its authority to detain non-citizens as enemy combatants with no federal court review stayed in place for the remainder of the Congress, since the courts' stripped jurisdiction was never restored by law.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania, senior Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it across party lines.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Held committee hearings, ordered the bill reported favorably, and reported it to the Senate without amendment.

for.name: 30 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent senator
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including future President Barack Obama and Senators Biden, Clinton, and Kerry.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never called the bill up from the Senate calendar for a floor vote during the remaining 18 months of the 110th Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration defended the Military Commissions Act's stripping of detainee court access and opposed restoring habeas for Guantanamo detainees.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican Judiciary leader joined by 30 Democrats and 1 Independent — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so the record shows no roll call revealing how the parties would have divided.

industries.industry: Executive branch detention and military-commissions system
industries.note: The bill re-subjects the government's detention of enemy combatants to federal court review, ending the no-review arrangement the Military Commissions Act created. Courts could order releases or force the government to justify every detention.
